claim: Local interneurons (LNs) mediate complex interactions within the antennal lobe, the primary olfactory system of insects.
source: Local interneurons (LNs) mediate complex interactions within the antennal lobe, the primary olfactory system of insects, and the functional analog of the vertebrate olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is a general statement about LN function that draws from established scientific understanding of the insect olfactory system.

claim: The antennal lobe is the functional analog of the vertebrate olfactory bulb.
source: Local interneurons (LNs) mediate complex interactions within the antennal lobe, the primary olfactory system of insects, and the functional analog of the vertebrate olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is a well-established comparison in the field based on structural and functional similarities.

claim: In Periplaneta americana, several types of LNs with distinctive physiological and morphological properties can be defined.
source: In the cockroach Periplaneta americana, as in other insects, several types of LNs with distinctive physiological and morphological properties can be defined.
evidence: This statement is supported by previous research and is confirmed by the experimental observations in this study.

claim: Spiking GABAergic LNs reacted to odorant stimulation with a uniform rise in [Ca2+]i in the ramifications of all innervated glomeruli.
source: Spiking GABAergic LNs reacted to odorant stimulation with a uniform rise in [Ca2+]i in the ramifications of all innervated glomeruli.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly supported by the calcium imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In nonspiking LNs, glomerular Ca2+ signals were odorant specific and varied between glomeruli.
source: In contrast, in nonspiking LNs, glomerular Ca2+ signals were odorant specific and varied between glomeruli, resulting in distinct, glomerulus-specific tuning curves.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly supported by the calcium imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nonspiking LNs exhibit distinct, glomerulus-specific tuning curves.
source: In contrast, in nonspiking LNs, glomerular Ca2+ signals were odorant specific and varied between glomeruli, resulting in distinct, glomerulus-specific tuning curves.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly supported by the calcium imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spiking LNs play a primary role in interglomerular signaling.
source: The cell type-specific differences in Ca2+ dynamics support the idea that spiking LNs play a primary role in interglomerular signaling, while they assign nonspiking LNs an essential role in intraglomerular signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed calcium dynamics data and their functional implications.

claim: Nonspiking LNs play an essential role in intraglomerular signaling.
source: The cell type-specific differences in Ca2+ dynamics support the idea that spiking LNs play a primary role in interglomerular signaling, while they assign nonspiking LNs an essential role in intraglomerular signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed calcium dynamics data and their functional implications.

claim: The antennal lobe shows striking structural and functional similarities to the vertebrates' olfactory bulb.
source: The AL is the first synaptic relay in the insect olfactory system, showing striking structural and functional similarities to the vertebrates' olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is based on established comparative neuroscience knowledge.

claim: LNs in the antennal lobe are the functional equivalent of granule cells, periglomerular cells, and short axon cells in the vertebrate olfactory bulb.
source: In many regards, the LNs in the AL are the functional equivalent of granule cells, but also periglomerular and short axon cells in the vertebrate olfactory bulb (Ennis et al., 2015; Shepherd et al., 2004).
evidence: This comparison is supported by cited references.

claim: LNs help to structure the odor representation in the antennal lobe.
source: They help to structure the odor representation in the AL, ultimately shaping the tuning profiles of the olfactory projection (output) neurons.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of LN function in olfactory processing.

claim: LNs shape the tuning profiles of olfactory projection neurons.
source: They help to structure the odor representation in the AL, ultimately shaping the tuning profiles of the olfactory projection (output) neurons.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of LN function in olfactory processing.

claim: LNs have been originally characterized as GABAergic and multiglomerular.
source: Based on initial studies, LNs originally have been characterized as GABAergic and multiglomerular (Distler, 1989; Hoskins et al., 1986; Waldrop et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by cited historical references.

claim: LNs can generate Na+-driven action potentials.
source: Typically, they can generate Na+-driven action potentials (Chou et al., 2010; Christensen et al., 1993; Husch et al., 2009a; Seki et al., 2010) or Ca2+-driven spikelets (Laurent and Davidowitz, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: LNs can generate Ca2+-driven spikelets.
source: Typically, they can generate Na+-driven action potentials (Chou et al., 2010; Christensen et al., 1993; Husch et al., 2009a; Seki et al., 2010) or Ca2+-driven spikelets (Laurent and Davidowitz, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: LNs have been associated with inhibitory interglomerular signaling.
source: Accordingly, these neurons have been associated with inhibitory interglomerular signaling, that is, with mediating lateral inhibition to enhance contrast and to control timing and synchronization of neuronal activity (Assisi and Bazhenov, 2012; Assisi et al., 2011; Christensen et al., 1998; Fujiwara et al., 2014; Hong and Wilson, 2015; MacLeod and Laurent, 1996; Nagel and Wilson, 2016; Olsen and Wilson, 2008; Sachse and Galizia, 2002; Wilson, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: LNs mediate lateral inhibition to enhance contrast.
source: Accordingly, these neurons have been associated with inhibitory interglomerular signaling, that is, with mediating lateral inhibition to enhance contrast and to control timing and synchronization of neuronal activity (Assisi and Bazhenov, 2012; Assisi et al., 2011; Christensen et al., 1998; Fujiwara et al., 2014; Hong and Wilson, 2015; MacLeod and Laurent, 1996; Nagel and Wilson, 2016; Olsen and Wilson, 2008; Sachse and Galizia, 2002; Wilson, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: LNs control timing and synchronization of neuronal activity.
source: Accordingly, these neurons have been associated with inhibitory interglomerular signaling, that is, with mediating lateral inhibition to enhance contrast and to control timing and synchronization of neuronal activity (Assisi and Bazhenov, 2012; Assisi et al., 2011; Christensen et al., 1998; Fujiwara et al., 2014; Hong and Wilson, 2015; MacLeod and Laurent, 1996; Nagel and Wilson, 2016; Olsen and Wilson, 2008; Sachse and Galizia, 2002; Wilson, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: LNs can synthesize neurotransmitters and neuromodulators other than GABA.
source: Subsequent studies showed that LNs can also synthesize other potential neurotransmitters and neuromodulators (Berg et al., 2007; Chou et al., 2010; Das et al., 2011; Distler, 1990; Fusca et al., 2013; Fusca et al., 2015; Neupert et al., 2012; Shang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: LNs can be excitatory.
source: In fact, they can be excitatory, distributing excitatory synaptic input to (projection) neurons in other glomeruli by chemical and electrical synapses (Assisi et al., 2012; Das et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2010; Olsen et al., 2007; Shang et al., 2007; Yaksi and Wilson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: LNs distribute excitatory synaptic input to neurons in other glomeruli by chemical and electrical synapses.
source: In fact, they can be excitatory, distributing excitatory synaptic input to (projection) neurons in other glomeruli by chemical and electrical synapses (Assisi et al., 2012; Das et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2010; Olsen et al., 2007; Shang et al., 2007; Yaksi and Wilson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Nonspiking LNs with weak active membrane properties that do not generate Na+-driven action potentials have been described in both holo- and hemimetabolous insect species.
source: Furthermore, nonspiking LNs with weak active membrane properties that do not generate Na+-driven action potentials have been described in both holo- and hemimetabolous insect species (Fuscà and Kloppenburg, 2021; Husch et al., 2009a; Husch et al., 2009b; Tabuchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: The functional role of nonspiking LNs for odor information processing is not clear yet.
source: While their functional role for odor information processing is not clear yet, it is plausible to assume that they are functionally highly relevant since they have been found across different insect species.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current understanding.

claim: Nonspiking LNs are functionally highly relevant since they have been found across different insect species.
source: While their functional role for odor information processing is not clear yet, it is plausible to assume that they are functionally highly relevant since they have been found across different insect species.
evidence: This is an inference based on their widespread occurrence across species.

claim: In Periplaneta americana, two main LN types have been identified: spiking type I LNs and nonspiking type II LNs.
source: In Periplaneta americana, two main LN types, each with distinct functional properties, have been identified: spiking type I LNs and nonspiking type II LNs (Fusca et al., 2013; Fuscà and Kloppenburg, 2021; Husch et al., 2009a; Husch et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Spiking type I LNs generate Na+-driven action potentials upon odor stimulation.
source: Spiking type I LNs generate Na+-driven action potentials upon odor stimulation and have a multiglomerular branching pattern with ramifications in many, but not all, glomeruli.
evidence: This is a characteristic feature of type I LNs supported by previous studies.

claim: Type I LNs have a multiglomerular branching pattern with ramifications in many, but not all, glomeruli.
source: Spiking type I LNs generate Na+-driven action potentials upon odor stimulation and have a multiglomerular branching pattern with ramifications in many, but not all, glomeruli.
evidence: This is a morphological characteristic supported by previous studies and confirmed by the data in this manuscript.

claim: The density and pattern of ramifications vary between glomeruli in type I LNs from very dense to sparse.
source: The density and pattern of ramifications vary between glomeruli from very dense to sparse, indicating a polarity with defined synaptic input and output regions.
evidence: This is a morphological observation that supports functional interpretations.

claim: The variable density of ramifications in type I LNs indicates a polarity with defined synaptic input and output regions.
source: The density and pattern of ramifications vary between glomeruli from very dense to sparse, indicating a polarity with defined synaptic input and output regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological observations.

claim: All type I LNs are GABAergic.
source: All type I LNs are GABAergic (Distler, 1989; Husch et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Nonspiking type II LNs do not have voltage-activated transient Na+ currents.
source: The nonspiking type II LNs do not have voltage-activated transient Na+ currents and cannot generate Na+-driven action potentials.
evidence: This is a physiological characteristic of type II LNs.

claim: Type II LNs cannot generate Na+-driven action potentials.
source: The nonspiking type II LNs do not have voltage-activated transient Na+ currents and cannot generate Na+-driven action potentials.
evidence: This is a physiological characteristic of type II LNs.

claim: Type II LNs have comparatively large voltage-dependent Ca2+ conductances.
source: They have comparatively large voltage-dependent Ca2+ conductances, which play a crucial role in mediating their active membrane properties (Fusca et al., 2013; Husch et al., 2009a; Husch et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Voltage-dependent Ca2+ conductances play a crucial role in mediating the active membrane properties of type II LNs.
source: They have comparatively large voltage-dependent Ca2+ conductances, which play a crucial role in mediating their active membrane properties (Fusca et al., 2013; Husch et al., 2009a; Husch et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Type II LNs consist of two main subtypes: type IIa and type IIb LNs.
source: Type II LNs consist of two main subtypes, type IIa and type IIb LNs.
evidence: This is a classification based on previous studies.

claim: Type IIa LNs typically respond with complex, odor-specific patterns of excitation that can include periods of inhibition.
source: Type IIa LNs typically respond with complex, odor-specific patterns of excitation that can include periods of inhibition.
evidence: This is a physiological characteristic of type IIa LNs.

claim: Type IIa LNs can be further subdivided into type IIa1 and type IIa2.
source: Type IIa LNs can be further subdivided into type IIa1 and type IIa2.
evidence: This is a classification based on previous studies.

claim: Type IIa1 LNs are cholinergic.
source: Type IIa1 LNs are cholinergic and can generate Ca2+-driven spikelets on top of odor-induced depolarizations (Fusca et al., 2013; Neupert et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Type IIa1 LNs can generate Ca2+-driven spikelets on top of odor-induced depolarizations.
source: Type IIa1 LNs are cholinergic and can generate Ca2+-driven spikelets on top of odor-induced depolarizations (Fusca et al., 2013; Neupert et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Type IIa2 LNs do not generate spikelets.
source: Type IIa2 LNs do not generate spikelets, and their primary transmitter is not known.
evidence: This is a physiological characteristic of type IIa2 LNs.

claim: The primary transmitter of type IIa2 LNs is not known.
source: Type IIa2 LNs do not generate spikelets, and their primary transmitter is not known.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Type IIb LNs have weak active membrane properties.
source: Type IIb LNs have weak active membrane properties and respond to odor stimulation with sustained, relatively smooth depolarization.
evidence: This is a physiological characteristic of type IIb LNs.

claim: Type IIb LNs respond to odor stimulation with sustained, relatively smooth depolarization.
source: Type IIb LNs have weak active membrane properties and respond to odor stimulation with sustained, relatively smooth depolarization.
evidence: This is a physiological characteristic of type IIb LNs.

claim: The primary transmitter of type IIb LNs is unknown.
source: Their primary transmitter is unknown.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: All type II LNs are omniglomerular, with branches in virtually all glomeruli.
source: All type II LNs are omniglomerular, with branches in virtually all glomeruli.
evidence: This is a morphological characteristic supported by previous studies and confirmed by the data in this manuscript.

claim: The density and pattern of arborizations are similar in all glomeruli of a given type II LN but vary between different type II LNs.
source: The density and pattern of arborizations are similar in all glomeruli of a given type II LN but vary between different type II LNs (Husch et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is a morphological observation supported by a cited reference.

claim: In type IIa LNs, the ramifications are similar and evenly distributed over each glomerulus of an individual neuron.
source: In type IIa LNs, the ramifications are similar and evenly distributed over each glomerulus of an individual neuron.
evidence: This is a morphological characteristic of type IIa LNs.

claim: In type IIb neurons, the branches cover only parts of each glomerulus, often in a specific layer.
source: On the other hand, in type IIb neurons, the branches cover only parts of each glomerulus, often in a specific layer (Husch et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is a morphological characteristic supported by a cited reference.

claim: Nonspiking type II LNs are primarily involved in intraglomerular signaling.
source: Based on their functional and morphological properties, it can be hypothesized that nonspiking type II LNs are primarily involved in intraglomerular signaling since the graded changes in membrane potentials can only spread within the same or electrotonically close glomeruli, as was proposed for nonspiking LNs in the rabbit olfactory bulb (Bufler et al., 1992b).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on functional and morphological properties, supported by a cited reference from a related system.

claim: Graded changes in membrane potentials in nonspiking LNs can only spread within the same or electrotonically close glomeruli.
source: Based on their functional and morphological properties, it can be hypothesized that nonspiking type II LNs are primarily involved in intraglomerular signaling since the graded changes in membrane potentials can only spread within the same or electrotonically close glomeruli, as was proposed for nonspiking LNs in the rabbit olfactory bulb (Bufler et al., 1992b).
evidence: This is based on biophysical principles and supported by a cited reference.

claim: Type I LNs are GABAergic and inhibitory.
source: Spiking type I LNs are GABAergic, inhibitory, and innervate many but not all glomeruli.
evidence: This is based on previous studies and is consistent with the data in this manuscript.

claim: Type I LNs innervate many but not all glomeruli.
source: Spiking type I LNs are GABAergic, inhibitory, and innervate many but not all glomeruli.
evidence: This is a morphological characteristic confirmed by the data in this manuscript.

claim: Some glomeruli are densely innervated by type I LNs, while others are more sparsely or not at all innervated.
source: While some glomeruli are densely innervated, others are more sparsely or not at all innervated (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the morphological data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The variable innervation pattern of type I LNs reflects an organization with distinctive input and output glomeruli.
source: It has been considered that this reflects an organization with distinctive input and output glomeruli (Galizia and Kimmerle, 2004; Husch et al., 2009a; Wilson and Laurent, 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by cited references.

claim: In type I LNs, synaptic input is integrated and triggers action potential firing.
source: In this model, synaptic input is integrated and triggers action potential firing.
evidence: This is part of a functional model based on the properties of type I LNs.

claim: Action potentials in type I LNs propagate to the innervated glomeruli and provide a defined glomeruli array with inhibitory synaptic input.
source: The action potentials propagate to the innervated glomeruli and provide a defined glomeruli array with inhibitory synaptic input.
evidence: This is part of a functional model based on the properties of type I LNs.

claim: Glomeruli can interact independently of their spatial and electrotonic distance via type I LNs.
source: Glomeruli can interact independently of their spatial and electrotonic distance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the action potential-mediated signaling in type I LNs.

claim: Odor-evoked glomerular Ca2+ signals in type I LNs are dominated by Ca2+ influx through voltage-gated channels activated by action potentials.
source: In this scenario, one would expect that odor-evoked glomerular Ca2+ signals are dominated by Ca2+ influx through voltage-gated channels that are activated by the action potentials.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the functional model, which is confirmed by the experimental data.

claim: Odor-induced Ca2+ signals in type I LNs should be detectable and comparable in all innervated glomeruli.
source: Thus, odor-induced Ca2+ signals should be detectable and comparable in all innervated glomeruli.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the functional model, which is confirmed by the experimental data.

claim: Type II LNs have very similar branching patterns in all glomeruli.
source: In contrast, nonspiking type II LNs have very similar branching patterns in all glomeruli (Figure 1B, Husch et al., 2009b), suggesting that both input and output can occur in every glomerulus.
evidence: This is a morphological observation supported by Figure 1B and a cited reference.

claim: The similar branching patterns in type II LNs suggest that both input and output can occur in every glomerulus.
source: In contrast, nonspiking type II LNs have very similar branching patterns in all glomeruli (Figure 1B, Husch et al., 2009b), suggesting that both input and output can occur in every glomerulus.
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological observations.

claim: Synaptic input during olfactory stimulation typically occurs only in a limited number of glomeruli.
source: Due to the receptor and sensillum type-specific input configuration of the glomeruli in the AL (Fujimura et al., 1991; Watanabe et al., 2012), synaptic input during olfactory stimulation typically occurs only in a limited number of glomeruli (Sachse et al., 1999; Silbering et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on cited references about the organization of olfactory input.

claim: Stimulus-evoked graded postsynaptic potentials in type II LNs can only spread within the same glomerulus or electrotonically nearby glomeruli.
source: The resulting stimulus-evoked graded postsynaptic potentials can only spread within the same glomerulus or electrotonically nearby glomeruli.
evidence: This is based on biophysical principles of signal propagation in nonspiking neurons.

claim: Ca2+ signals in type II LNs are dominated by odorant-evoked Ca2+ influx through excitatory ligand-gated channels.
source: Since these neurons cannot generate Na+-driven action potentials, we hypothesize that the Ca2+ signals are dominated by odorant-evoked Ca2+ influx through excitatory ligand-gated channels (Oliveira et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the physiological properties of type II LNs, supported by a cited reference.

claim: This study is based on 23 recordings of type I LNs and 18 recordings of type II LNs.
source: Overall, this study is based on 23 recordings of type I LNs and 18 recordings of type II LNs.
evidence: This is a statement about the sample size of the study.

claim: For each recorded LN, between 9 and 25 distinct innervated glomeruli could be identified and individually imaged and analyzed.
source: For each recorded LN, between 9 and 25 distinct innervated glomeruli could be identified and individually imaged and analyzed.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology and data collection.

claim: The odor-induced Ca2+ dynamics were highly reproducible when the antennae were repeatedly stimulated with the same odorant.
source: In the first set of experiments, we showed that the odor-induced Ca2+ dynamics were highly reproducible when the antennae were repeatedly stimulated with the same odorant (Figure 2).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: LNs responded very reproducibly to repeated olfactory stimulations in previous electrophysiological studies.
source: This is in line with previous electrophysiological studies, in which LNs responded very reproducibly to repeated olfactory stimulations (Husch et al., 2009a; Husch et al., 2009b; Olsen and Wilson, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: All recorded type I LNs displayed characteristic morphological features with arborizations in multiple glomeruli with varying neurite densities between glomeruli.
source: All recorded type I LNs displayed characteristic morphological features, that is, arborizations in multiple glomeruli with varying neurite densities between glomeruli (Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in the morphological data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Type I LNs reacted to odor stimulation with odorant-specific patterns of overshooting action potentials.
source: Electrophysiologically, type I LNs reacted to odor stimulation of the antennae with odorant-specific patterns of overshooting action potentials (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The glomerular Ca2+ signals in type I LNs were time-locked with the electrophysiological responses.
source: The glomerular Ca2+ signals were time-locked with the electrophysiological responses and matched the spike pattern of the electrophysiological recordings.
evidence: This is directly observed in the combined electrophysiological and imaging data.

claim: The glomerular Ca2+ signals in type I LNs matched the spike pattern of the electrophysiological recordings.
source: The glomerular Ca2+ signals were time-locked with the electrophysiological responses and matched the spike pattern of the electrophysiological recordings.
evidence: This is directly observed in the combined electrophysiological and imaging data.

claim: While the absolute amplitudes of the Ca2+ signals varied between individual glomeruli in type I LNs, the time course and overall structure of the Ca2+ signals were very similar in all recorded glomeruli for a particular odorant.
source: While the absolute amplitudes of the Ca2+ signals during a given odorant varied between individual glomeruli, the time course and overall structure of the Ca2+ signals were very similar in all recorded glomeruli for a particular odorant (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), resulting in identical tuning curves for all glomeruli of a given neuron (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the imaging data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The similar Ca2+ dynamics across glomeruli in type I LNs resulted in identical tuning curves for all glomeruli of a given neuron.
source: While the absolute amplitudes of the Ca2+ signals during a given odorant varied between individual glomeruli, the time course and overall structure of the Ca2+ signals were very similar in all recorded glomeruli for a particular odorant (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), resulting in identical tuning curves for all glomeruli of a given neuron (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the tuning curve data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Tuning curves of all imaged glomeruli of a given type I LN always correlated with coefficients of ~1.
source: Accordingly, tuning curves of all imaged glomeruli of a given neuron always correlated with coefficients of ~1, with a mean correlation coefficient across all investigated spiking LNs of r = 0.95 ± 0.06 (N = 16, Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is directly calculated from the tuning curve data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: The mean correlation coefficient across all investigated spiking type I LNs was r = 0.95 ± 0.06 (N = 16).
source: Accordingly, tuning curves of all imaged glomeruli of a given neuron always correlated with coefficients of ~1, with a mean correlation coefficient across all investigated spiking LNs of r = 0.95 ± 0.06 (N = 16, Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the correlation data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: When action potential generation in type I LNs was inhibited by hyperpolarization, the neurons responded with odorant-specific graded depolarizations.
source: When the generation of action potentials is inhibited, the remaining Ca2+ signals should mainly reflect Ca2+ influx via ligand-gated channels (e.g., cholinergic receptors, Oliveira et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a prediction that is confirmed by the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: When action potential firing was prevented by hyperpolarization in type I LNs, odor stimulation still elicited Ca2+ signals in the glomeruli.
source: When action potential firing was prevented by hyperpolarization, odor stimulation still elicited Ca2+ signals in the glomeruli (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When action potential firing was prevented in type I LNs, the uniformity of the Ca2+ signals between different glomeruli disappeared.
source: Besides a reduction in amplitude, the uniformity of the Ca2+ signals between different glomeruli disappeared.
evidence: This is directly observed in the imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: When action potential firing was prevented in type I LNs, the tuning curves of the individual glomeruli became different from each other.
source: In turn, the tuning curves of the individual glomeruli became different from each other (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the tuning curve data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mean correlation coefficient across all hyperpolarized type I LNs was r = 0.75 ± 0.19 (N = 6).
source: Quantitatively, this is reflected in the glomerulus-specific odorant responses and the diverse correlations between the glomerular tuning curves, resulting in a decreased mean correlation coefficient across all hyperpolarized type I LNs of r = 0.75 ± 0.19 (N = 6, Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the correlation data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: When action potential firing was suppressed by intracellularly blocking Na+ channels with QX-314 in type I LNs, similar results were obtained as with hyperpolarization (r = 0.74 ± 0.26, N = 5).
source: Similar results were obtained when action potential firing was suppressed by intracellularly blocking Na+ channels with QX-314 (r = 0.74 ± 0.26, N = 5, Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the correlation data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Differences in mean correlation coefficients were significant between control and hyperpolarized type I LNs (p=0.0073).
source: Differences in mean correlation coefficients were significant between control and hyperpolarized type I LNs (p=0.0073) as well as between control and type I LNs that were treated with QX-314 (p=0.0142).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison of experimental conditions.

claim: Differences in mean correlation coefficients were significant between control and type I LNs that were treated with QX-314 (p=0.0142).
source: Differences in mean correlation coefficients were significant between control and hyperpolarized type I LNs (p=0.0073) as well as between control and type I LNs that were treated with QX-314 (p=0.0142).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison of experimental conditions.

claim: Mean correlation coefficients of hyperpolarized and QX-314-treated type I LNs were not significantly different (p>0.999).
source: Mean correlation coefficients of hyperpolarized and QX-314-treated type I LNs were not significantly different (p>0.999).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison of experimental conditions.

claim: The observed large Ca2+ signals in type I LNs are mediated mainly by voltage-gated Ca2+ channels activated by action potentials.
source: These experiments support the idea that the observed large Ca2+ signals are mediated mainly by voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, which are activated by the strong depolarizations of the action potentials propagating through the neuron into the innervated glomeruli.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental results with hyperpolarization and QX-314 treatment.

claim: Large Ca2+ signals in type I LNs likely mask small local Ca2+ signals elicited by ligand-gated (postsynaptic) Ca2+ influx.
source: These large signals likely mask small local Ca2+ signals elicited by ligand-gated (postsynaptic) Ca2+ influx into the recorded neuron.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing different Ca2+ dynamics when action potentials are suppressed.

claim: Preventing the generation of action potentials selectively in type I LNs unmasked small local Ca2+ signals, which are interpreted as evidence for localized excitatory input.
source: Preventing the generation of action potentials selectively in the recorded neurons unmasked small local Ca2+ signals, which we interpret as solid evidence for localized excitatory input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results with hyperpolarization and QX-314 treatment.

claim: Individual type I LNs receive excitatory input in multiple glomeruli.
source: Since we observed these signals in more than one glomerulus of a given neuron, we consider this to be physiological evidence that individual type I LNs receive excitatory input not only in one but in multiple glomeruli.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation of localized Ca2+ signals in multiple glomeruli when action potentials are suppressed.

claim: Type I LNs integrate and transform their synaptic input to action potential firing to provide inhibitory synaptic input (lateral inhibition) to neurons in a defined array of glomeruli.
source: Taken together, our results are in line with the conception that type I LNs integrate and transform their synaptic input to action potential firing to provide inhibitory synaptic input (lateral inhibition) to neurons in a defined array of glomeruli (Assisi et al., 2011; Fujiwara et al., 2014; Hong and Wilson, 2015; Nagel and Wilson, 2016; Olsen and Wilson, 2008; Sachse and Galizia, 2002; Wilson, 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and supported by cited references.

claim: An individual type I LN receives excitatory input not only in one but in several glomeruli, which is in line with previous structural and ultrastructural studies.
source: Our results also provide physiological evidence that an individual type I LN receives excitatory input not only in one but in several glomeruli, which is in line with previous structural- and ultrastructural studies that reported evidence for both pre- and postsynaptic profiles in individual glomeruli (Berck et al., 2016; Distler and Boeckh, 1997b; Mohamed et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and supported by cited references.

claim: Highly heterogeneous Ca2+ dynamics were observed between individual glomeruli in most type II LNs.
source: In contrast to the uniform Ca2+ dynamics during odor stimulation in type I LNs, we observed highly heterogeneous Ca2+ dynamics between the individual glomeruli in most type II LNs (Figure 5).
evidence: This is directly observed in the imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: All recorded type II LNs had the cell type-specific morphology characterized by innervation of all glomeruli with similar neurite densities in all glomeruli of a given neuron.
source: All recorded type II LNs had the cell type-specific morphology characterized by innervation of all glomeruli with similar neurite densities in all glomeruli of a given neuron (Figure 5A and E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the morphological data shown in Figure 5A and E.

claim: All type II LNs typically responded with graded changes in membrane potential to olfactory stimulation.
source: All type II LNs typically responded with graded changes in membrane potential to olfactory stimulation, with type IIa1 LNs also able to generate Ca2+-driven spikelets (Figure 5B and F, top traces).

claim: Type IIa1 LNs are able to generate Ca2+-driven spikelets.

claim: The amplitudes of the Ca2+ signals in type II LNs were in the range of the signals of type I LNs after the suppression of their action potentials.
source: The amplitudes of the corresponding Ca2+ signals were in the range of the signals of type I LNs after the suppression of their action potentials.
evidence: This is a comparison of the imaging data from type II LNs and hyperpolarized type I LNs.

claim: While the electrophysiological responses to different odorants were similar in a given type II LN, the corresponding glomerular Ca2+ signals were odor specific and varied between glomeruli.
source: While the electrophysiological responses to different odorants were similar in a given neuron, the corresponding glomerular Ca2+ signals were odor specific and varied between glomeruli, resulting in distinct, glomerulus-specific tuning curves (Figure 5C,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which was also directly evident in a relatively low degree of correlation (Figure 5I; r = 0.56 ± 0.21, N = 18).
evidence: This is directly observed in the combined electrophysiological and imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mean correlation coefficient across all investigated type II LNs was r = 0.56 ± 0.21 (N = 18).
source: While the electrophysiological responses to different odorants were similar in a given neuron, the corresponding glomerular Ca2+ signals were odor specific and varied between glomeruli, resulting in distinct, glomerulus-specific tuning curves (Figure 5C,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which was also directly evident in a relatively low degree of correlation (Figure 5I; r = 0.56 ± 0.21, N = 18).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the correlation data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The correlation between tuning curves of individual glomeruli in a given type II LN differed among type II LNs.

claim: In 11 out of 18 nonspiking LNs, the majority of glomeruli was individually tuned.
source: While in 11 out of 18 nonspiking LNs the majority of glomeruli was individually tuned, in the other 7 neurons, groups of similarly tuned glomeruli were found.
evidence: This is a summary of the tuning curve analysis across all type II LNs.

claim: In 7 out of 18 nonspiking LNs, groups of similarly tuned glomeruli were found.
source: While in 11 out of 18 nonspiking LNs the majority of glomeruli was individually tuned, in the other 7 neurons, groups of similarly tuned glomeruli were found.
evidence: This is a summary of the tuning curve analysis across all type II LNs.

claim: Groups of similarly tuned glomeruli in some type II LNs could be caused by similar input to several glomeruli.
source: Mechanistically, this could be caused by similar input to several glomeruli (Watanabe et al., 2012) or by coordinated activity, for example, via spikelets that were observed in a subtype of nonspiking neurons (type IIa1 LNs, Fusca et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed correlation patterns, supported by cited references.

claim: Groups of similarly tuned glomeruli in some type II LNs could be caused by coordinated activity via spikelets.
source: Mechanistically, this could be caused by similar input to several glomeruli (Watanabe et al., 2012) or by coordinated activity, for example, via spikelets that were observed in a subtype of nonspiking neurons (type IIa1 LNs, Fusca et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed correlation patterns, supported by cited references.

claim: In the cockroach antennal lobe, sensory inputs are processed and computed in inter- and intraglomerular circuits formed by spiking type I and nonspiking type II LNs.
source: We conclude that in the cockroach AL sensory inputs are processed and computed in inter- and intraglomerular circuits, which are formed by spiking type I and nonspiking type II LNs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental results.

claim: Processing of olfactory information in the antennal lobe involves complex interactions between the glomerular pathways and between different AL neurons.
source: Processing of olfactory information in the AL involves complex interactions between the glomerular pathways and between different AL neurons.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of olfactory processing.

claim: GABAergic LNs can mediate lateral inhibition by providing inhibitory synaptic input to defined odor-specific arrays of glomeruli.
source: Previous studies in different insect species have suggested that GABAergic LNs can mediate lateral inhibition by providing inhibitory synaptic input to defined odor-specific arrays of glomeruli.
evidence: This is based on previous studies in the field.

claim: Type I LNs express GABA-like immunoreactivity.
source: Since type I LNs express GABA-like immunoreactivity and provide inhibitory input to uPNs and other LNs in all innervated glomeruli (Distler, 1989; Distler and Boeckh, 1997b; Husch et al., 2009a; Warren and Kloppenburg, 2014), these neurons are likely part of an inhibitory network that mediates lateral inhibition and contrast enhancement (Sachse and Galizia, 2002; Wilson and Laurent, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Type I LNs provide inhibitory input to uPNs and other LNs in all innervated glomeruli.
source: Since type I LNs express GABA-like immunoreactivity and provide inhibitory input to uPNs and other LNs in all innervated glomeruli (Distler, 1989; Distler and Boeckh, 1997b; Husch et al., 2009a; Warren and Kloppenburg, 2014), these neurons are likely part of an inhibitory network that mediates lateral inhibition and contrast enhancement (Sachse and Galizia, 2002; Wilson and Laurent, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Type I LNs are likely part of an inhibitory network that mediates lateral inhibition and contrast enhancement.
source: Since type I LNs express GABA-like immunoreactivity and provide inhibitory input to uPNs and other LNs in all innervated glomeruli (Distler, 1989; Distler and Boeckh, 1997b; Husch et al., 2009a; Warren and Kloppenburg, 2014), these neurons are likely part of an inhibitory network that mediates lateral inhibition and contrast enhancement (Sachse and Galizia, 2002; Wilson and Laurent, 2005).
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of type I LNs and supported by cited references.

claim: The current study does not rule out the possibility that type I LNs are also involved in intraglomerular signaling.
source: While the current study assigns a role to type I LNs in interglomerular signaling, it does not rule out the possibility that these neurons are also involved in intraglomerular signaling.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study's conclusions.

claim: The experiments with suppressed action potential firing reveal that the hypothesized polar organization of type I LNs with strictly defined input and output glomeruli is not entirely correct.
source: In this context, the experiments with suppressed action potential firing reveal an additional functional aspect of type I LNs. They indicate that the hypothesized polar organization of type I LNs with strictly defined (and separated) input and output glomeruli is not entirely correct.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental results with hyperpolarization and QX-314 treatment.

claim: When type I LNs were prevented from spiking, distinct, glomeruli-specific Ca2+ dynamics were observed during odor stimulation.
source: When type I LNs were prevented from spiking by hyperpolarization or intracellular block of Na+ channels, we observed distinct, glomeruli-specific Ca2+ dynamics during odor stimulation.
evidence: This is directly observed in the imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The glomeruli-specific Ca2+ signals in hyperpolarized type I LNs likely originate from Ca2+ influx through Ca2+ permeable excitatory receptors such as cholinergic receptors.
source: It is likely that these signals originate from Ca2+ influx through Ca2+ permeable excitatory receptors such as cholinergic receptors, suggesting that each neuron can potentially receive excitatory olfactory input in many innervated glomerulus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and supported by a cited reference.

claim: Each type I LN can potentially receive excitatory olfactory input in many innervated glomeruli.
source: It is likely that these signals originate from Ca2+ influx through Ca2+ permeable excitatory receptors such as cholinergic receptors, suggesting that each neuron can potentially receive excitatory olfactory input in many innervated glomerulus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: Individual GABAergic LNs receive broad, but not uniform, spatial patterns of excitation by either OSNs or PNs.
source: This notion agrees with previous studies in the fly, which suggested that individual GABAergic LNs receive broad, but not uniform, spatial patterns of excitation by either OSNs or PNs (Wilson and Laurent, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Most nonspiking type II LNs have distinct functional domains that are (more or less) independent from each other.
source: These heterogeneous and glomerulus-specific Ca2+ dynamics imply that type II LNs have distinct functional domains that are (more or less) independent from each other.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed heterogeneous Ca2+ dynamics.

claim: Most nonspiking type II LNs might contribute to microcircuits within glomeruli and mediate intraglomerular signaling rather than interconnecting multiple glomeruli.
source: Accordingly, most nonspiking type II LNs might contribute to microcircuits within glomeruli and mediate intraglomerular signaling rather than interconnecting multiple glomeruli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed heterogeneous Ca2+ dynamics.

claim: Intraglomerular circuits are known from the mouse or rat olfactory bulb.
source: Intraglomerular circuits are known from the mouse or rat olfactory bulb (for review, see Ennis et al., 2015), where periglomerular, external tufted, and short axon cells interact to modulate the output of Mitral/Tufted cells (Aungst et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2016; Najac et al., 2015; Wachowiak and Shipley, 2006).
evidence: This is based on cited references about the vertebrate olfactory bulb.

claim: Periglomerular, external tufted, and short axon cells interact to modulate the output of Mitral/Tufted cells in the vertebrate olfactory bulb.
source: Intraglomerular circuits are known from the mouse or rat olfactory bulb (for review, see Ennis et al., 2015), where periglomerular, external tufted, and short axon cells interact to modulate the output of Mitral/Tufted cells (Aungst et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2016; Najac et al., 2015; Wachowiak and Shipley, 2006).
evidence: This is based on cited references about the vertebrate olfactory bulb.

claim: Periglomerular cells are uniglomerular LNs that mediate intraglomerular synaptic signaling.
source: Periglomerular cells are uniglomerular LNs that mediate intraglomerular synaptic signaling.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of the vertebrate olfactory bulb.

claim: Cockroach type II LNs could serve similar purposes as periglomerular cells in the vertebrate olfactory bulb.
source: Unlike periglomerular cells, cockroach type II LNs innervate all glomeruli. Still, as these LNs have only weak active membrane properties, postsynaptic potentials just spread within the same glomerulus. Therefore, these neurons could serve similar purposes, and few omniglomerular type II LNs could perform similar functions as many PG uniglomerular cells.
evidence: This is a speculative comparison based on functional similarities.

claim: Few omniglomerular type II LNs could perform similar functions as many PG uniglomerular cells.
source: Unlike periglomerular cells, cockroach type II LNs innervate all glomeruli. Still, as these LNs have only weak active membrane properties, postsynaptic potentials just spread within the same glomerulus. Therefore, these neurons could serve similar purposes, and few omniglomerular type II LNs could perform similar functions as many PG uniglomerular cells.
evidence: This is a speculative comparison based on functional similarities.

claim: Nonspiking type II LNs are not a homogenous neuron population.
source: In addition, it is important to consider that nonspiking type II LNs are not a homogenous neuron population (Fusca et al., 2013; Husch et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: In a subpopulation of type II LNs, correlated Ca2+ dynamics were observed in subsets of glomeruli.
source: In a subpopulation of type II LNs, we observed correlated Ca2+ dynamics in subsets of glomeruli.
evidence: This is directly observed in the imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Subpopulations of type II LNs responded to odorant stimulations with strong depolarizations, including spikelets, which can propagate to a set of glomeruli.
source: Note that subpopulations of type II LNs responded to odorant stimulations with strong depolarizations, including spikelets, which apparently can propagate, at least to some extent, to a set of glomeruli.
evidence: This is directly observed in the electrophysiological and imaging data.

claim: Type IIa1 LNs are cholinergic and likely excitatory.
source: Since this subpopulation of nonspiking type II LNs (type IIa1 LNs) was previously shown to be cholinergic (Fusca et al., 2013; Neupert et al., 2018), they are likely excitatory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the neurotransmitter identity, supported by cited references.

claim: Cholinergic type IIa LNs might be part of an excitatory network that activates neurons in specific sets of glomeruli.
source: The intrinsic electrophysiological properties of the cholinergic type IIa LNs suggest that they might be part of an excitatory network, which activates neurons in specific sets of glomeruli.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the physiological properties of type IIa LNs.

claim: Excitatory LNs in the fruit fly, while being multiglomerular, only activate specific glomeruli, providing distinct arrays of glomeruli with excitatory input.
source: This hypothesis is in line with previous studies in the fruit fly, where excitatory LNs, while being multiglomerular, only activate specific glomeruli, thereby providing distinct arrays of glomeruli with excitatory input and distributing odor‐evoked activity over an ensemble of PNs (Das et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2010; Olsen et al., 2007; Root et al., 2007; Shang et al., 2007; reviewed in Wilson, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: The primary transmitter of most type II LNs is yet to be revealed.
source: While type IIa1 are cholinergic and type II LNs generally express multiple neuropeptides (Fusca et al., 2015; Neupert et al., 2012; Neupert et al., 2018), the primary transmitter of most type II LNs is yet to be revealed.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Type II LNs generally express multiple neuropeptides.
source: While type IIa1 are cholinergic and type II LNs generally express multiple neuropeptides (Fusca et al., 2015; Neupert et al., 2012; Neupert et al., 2018), the primary transmitter of most type II LNs is yet to be revealed.
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Glutamate is a candidate primary transmitter for type II LNs.
source: One candidate is glutamate, an inhibitory transmitter in the Drosophila AL (Liu and Wilson, 2013) and cockroach metathoracic motor neurons (Sattelle, 1992).
evidence: This is a speculation based on cited references about glutamate function in related systems.

claim: Glutamate is an inhibitory transmitter in the Drosophila antennal lobe.
source: One candidate is glutamate, an inhibitory transmitter in the Drosophila AL (Liu and Wilson, 2013) and cockroach metathoracic motor neurons (Sattelle, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Glutamate is an inhibitory transmitter in cockroach metathoracic motor neurons.
source: One candidate is glutamate, an inhibitory transmitter in the Drosophila AL (Liu and Wilson, 2013) and cockroach metathoracic motor neurons (Sattelle, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: The olfactory system's circuitry in Periplaneta americana has been analyzed in great detail on the physiological, biochemical, and structural/ultrastructural levels.
source: This is an experimental system in which the olfactory system's circuitry has been analyzed in great detail on the physiological (Bradler C et al., 2016; Ernst and Boeckh, 1983; Husch et al., 2009a; Husch et al., 2009b; Lemon, 1997, Lemon and Getz, 1998, Lemon and Getz, 2000; Nishino et al., 2012, Nishino et al., 2018; Paeger et al., 2017; Paoli et al., 2020; Pippow et al., 2009; Strausfeld and Li, 1999; Warren and Kloppenburg, 2014; Watanabe et al., 2017), biochemical (Distler, 1989; Distler, 1990; Fusca et al., 2013; Fusca et al., 2015; Neupert et al., 2012; Neupert et al., 2018), and structural/ ultrastructural levels (Distler and Boeckh, 1997a; Distler and Boeckh, 1997b; Distler et al., 1998; Malun, 1991a; Malun, 1991b; Malun et al., 1993; Nishino et al., 2015; Watanabe et al., 2010), thus contributing very successfully to understanding olfactory information processing principles.
evidence: This is supported by numerous cited references.

claim: The mean correlation coefficient of spiking type I LNs (0.95 ± 0.06, N = 16) is significantly larger compared to nonspiking type IIa1 LNs that can generate spikelets (0.67 ± 0.12, N = 6, p=0.01).
source: The mean correlation coefficient of spiking type I LNs (0.95 ± 0.06, N = 16) is significantly larger compared to nonspiking type IIa1 LNs that can generate spikelets (0.67 ± 0.12, N = 6, p=0.01) and (pooled) type IIa2 and type IIb LNs, which do not generate spikelets (0.51 ± 0.23, N = 12, p<0.001) (Kruskal–Wallis and Dunn's multiple comparisons tests).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison of different LN types shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The mean correlation coefficient of spiking type I LNs (0.95 ± 0.06, N = 16) is significantly larger compared to (pooled) type IIa2 and type IIb LNs, which do not generate spikelets (0.51 ± 0.23, N = 12, p<0.001).

evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison of different LN types shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Processing of sensory input by networks of spiking and nonspiking interneurons is a common principle in both invertebrate and vertebrate sensory systems.
source: Processing of sensory input by networks of spiking and nonspiking interneurons is a common principle in both invertebrate and vertebrate sensory systems, for example, structuring the signal pathway from sensory neurons (tactile hairs) to intersegmental and motor neurons in the insect thoracic ganglion (Burrows, 1989; Pearson and Fourtner, 1975) and the mammalian olfactory bulb (Bufler et al., 1992a; Bufler et al., 1992b; Wellis and Scott, 1990) and retina (Diamond, 2017).
evidence: This is based on cited references from various sensory systems.

claim: In many systems, the role of nonspiking neurons is not well understood.
source: Nevertheless, in many systems, the role of nonspiking neurons is not well understood.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current understanding across multiple systems.
